questions.question: A linear program has variables $\boldsymbol{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$, technology matrix $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, right-hand side $\boldsymbol{b}\in\mathbb{R}^m$ and objective coefficients $\boldsymbol{c}\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Which format is the standard form of a linear program?

When a linear program is brought into standard form, each bound on a single variable is either a domain definition (removed by substituting the variable) or a constraint (kept as a row of $\boldsymbol{A}$). Which bounds count as domain definitions?
options: Only lower bounds $x_j\geq k$, for any real $k$; an upper bound $x_j\leq u$ stays a row.
Lower bounds $x_j\geq k$ and upper bounds $x_j\leq u$ alike, as each involves one variable.
Only the bounds $x_j\geq0$; a bound $x_j\geq k$ with $k\neq0$ stays a row of $\boldsymbol{A}$.
Only lower bounds $x_j\geq k$ with $k\geq0$; a negative lower bound stays a row.

questions.question: A linear program has a variable $x_3$ whose only bound is $x_3\leq2$. Instead of splitting $x_3$ as the standard-form conversion scheme does, a student substitutes $x_3=2-x_3'$ with $x_3'\geq0$, drops the bound $x_3\leq2$ and moves the constants to the right-hand side. Which assessment of this rewrite is correct?
options: It is wrong: an upper bound counts as a constraint, so $x_3\leq2$ must stay a row of $\boldsymbol{A}$.
It is correct: $x_3'\geq0$ holds exactly when $x_3\leq2$, so it gives an equivalent standard form.
It is wrong: $x_3'\geq0$ gives $x_3=2-x_3'\geq2$, the opposite of the bound $x_3\leq2$.
It is correct only if $\boldsymbol{b}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ still holds once the constants are on the right-hand side.

questions.question: A linear program $\min\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over a feasible region $V$ has optimal value $z^*$. It is rewritten as $\max -\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over the same $V$. How are the optimal solutions and the optimal value of the rewritten program related to the original ones?
options: The optimal solutions are the same and the optimal value is again $z^*$.
Each optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ becomes $-\boldsymbol{x}^*$, and the optimal value is $z^*$.
The optimal solutions are the same and the optimal value is $-z^*$.
The optimal solutions are the maximizers of $\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ over $V$, value $-z^*$.

questions.question: In the conversion to standard form a free variable $x_j\in\mathbb{R}$ is replaced by $x_j^{+}-x_j^{-}$ with $x_j^{+},x_j^{-}\geq0$. Which statement about the values that $x_j^{+}-x_j^{-}$ can take is correct?
options: Every real number equals $x_j^{+}-x_j^{-}$ for some $x_j^{+},x_j^{-}\geq0$, so the range $\mathbb{R}$ is kept.
The range $\mathbb{R}$ is kept only once the extra constraint $x_j^{+}x_j^{-}=0$ is added.
The range shrinks to $[0,\infty)$, since a difference of nonnegative numbers is nonnegative.
The range $\mathbb{R}$ is kept only if $x_j^{-}\leq0$ is required instead of $x_j^{-}\geq0$.

questions.question: Which of the following linear programs in the variables $x_1,x_2$ is in standard form?
While a linear program is brought into standard form, the equality constraint $3x_1-x_2=-2$ must be replaced by $\leq$-rows only. Which rows replace it?

In a linear program with $x_2\geq0$, the variable $x_1$ has the domain definition $x_1\geq-3$. For standard form, $x_1$ is replaced by a shifted variable $x_1'\geq0$ and the constants are moved to the right-hand side. What does the constraint $2x_1+x_2\leq4$ become?

A firm makes products 1, 2, 3 from resources R1 and R2. One unit of product 1 uses 2 units of R1 and 1 of R2, product 2 uses 4 of R1 and 3 of R2, product 3 uses 1 of R1 and 5 of R2. With $x_i\geq0$ the output of product $i$, the capacity rows are $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, one row per resource. Which gives the size and first row of $\boldsymbol{A}$?

A linear program minimizes $2x_1-5x_2$, where $x_1\geq0$ and $x_2$ is free. In standard form the objective is turned into a maximization and $x_2$ is replaced by $x_2^{+}-x_2^{-}$ with $x_2^{+},x_2^{-}\geq0$. Which objective results?

In the conversion to standard form, each equality row is replaced by a $\leq$-row and a $\geq$-row, and each $\geq$-row is then multiplied by $-1$. What do these two operations do to the set of feasible points?
options: The split enlarges it, as a point now has to satisfy only one of the two inequalities.
Nothing: a point satisfies the new rows exactly when it satisfies the old ones.
Multiplying by $-1$ reflects it in the origin, which must be undone after solving.
Multiplying by $-1$ replaces it by the points that violated the original $\geq$-row.

questions.question: A linear program has a variable $x_3$ whose only bound is $x_3\leq0$. How does the standard-form conversion scheme handle $x_3$?
options: Replace $x_3$ by $x_3^{+}$ with $x_3^{+}\geq0$, treating $x_3\leq0$ as its domain definition.
Multiply the bound by $-1$ to get $-x_3\geq0$ and use it as the domain definition $x_3\geq0$.
Replace $x_3$ by $x_3^{+}-x_3^{-}$ with $x_3^{+},x_3^{-}\geq0$ and keep the row $x_3^{+}-x_3^{-}\leq0$.
Replace $x_3$ by $x_3^{+}-x_3^{-}$ with $x_3^{+},x_3^{-}\geq0$ and drop the bound $x_3\leq0$.

questions.question: A linear program has constraints $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$ with $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and lower bounds $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{b}'$ with $\boldsymbol{b}'\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Which single system $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ describes the same feasible region?

A linear program in $x_1,x_2,x_3$ with $x_1\geq2$, $x_2$ free and $x_3\geq0$ is brought into standard form using $x_1=x_1'+2$ and $x_2=x_2^{+}-x_2^{-}$, all new variables nonnegative. The standard form has optimal solution $(x_1',x_2^{+},x_2^{-},x_3)=(1,0,4,3)$. Which point is optimal for the original program?

In a linear program the variable $x_2$ has the bounds $-1\leq x_2\leq5$. In standard form lower bounds are domain definitions and upper bounds are constraints. How are $x_2$ and its two bounds rewritten?

In a linear program with $x_1,x_2,x_3\geq0$, the constraint $2x_1+7\geq x_2-x_3$ must be written as a $\leq$-row with all variables on the left-hand side and the constant on the right-hand side. Which row results?

The linear program $\max -x_1+x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq-1$, $x_1-x_2\leq5$, $x_1\geq0$, $x_2\in\mathbb{R}$ has the unique optimal solution $(0,-1)$. In standard form only $x_2$ is changed, to $x_2^{+}-x_2^{-}$ with $x_2^{+},x_2^{-}\geq0$. Which points $(x_1,x_2^{+},x_2^{-})$ are optimal for the standard form?
options: Only $(0,0,1)$, since a unique optimum stays unique

questions.question: A linear program in standard form has $\boldsymbol{A}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$, and its domain definitions $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ are written as rows, giving the system $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\tilde{\boldsymbol{b}}$ with $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}=\begin{pmatrix}\boldsymbol{A}\\-\boldsymbol{I}_n\end{pmatrix}$. What is the rank of $\tilde{\boldsymbol{A}}$?
options: Always $n$, since the $n$ rows of $-\boldsymbol{I}_n$ are already linearly independent.
Always $m+n$, the number of rows, since every row is a different constraint.
$n$ only if $m\geq n$, since $\boldsymbol{A}$ needs at least $n$ rows to reach rank $n$.

questions.question: A linear program minimizes a linear objective in $x_1,x_2,x_3$ subject to $x_1+x_2-x_3\leq6$, $2x_1-x_3\geq1$, $x_1+x_2+x_3=5$, $x_1\geq0$, $-2\leq x_2\leq4$ and $x_3\leq3$. In standard form lower bounds are domain definitions, a variable without one is split, and upper bounds are rows. What is the size of $\boldsymbol{A}$ in the standard form?

The linear program $\min Z=2x_1+3x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\geq6$, $x_1\geq4$, $x_2\geq-1$ has minimum $11$ at $(7,-1)$. In standard form, $x_1=x_1'+4$ and $x_2=x_2'-1$, and the constant left in the objective is dropped. What is the optimal value of the resulting standard-form program?
